questions.prompt: A colleague says a CRM Analytics dashboard's numbers are a few hours behind the Opportunity records in Salesforce. Which of these is the most likely explanation, given how the platform is architected?
options: The dashboard's queries run live against Salesforce objects but get cached by the browser for a few hours
CRM Analytics works on datasets that are extracted and loaded on a schedule, and the dataset simply hasn't refreshed since those Opportunities changed
The user's profile doesn't have field-level security enabled for Amount
CRM Analytics dashboards always lag Salesforce by exactly 24 hours, by design
questions.explain: CRM Analytics dashboards query datasets, not live Salesforce records. A dataset is extracted and prepared on a schedule, so its data is only ever as current as the last successful load. A few hours of lag almost always means the dataset's refresh schedule, not the data itself, is the thing to check.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Salesforce's Data Cloud / Data 360 platform, per Chapter 1.
options: Data Cloud was renamed Data 360 in October 2025, but it is the same underlying platform
Data flows through data streams (ingest), data lake objects (store), data model objects (harmonize), and calculated insight objects (aggregate)
Identity resolution, calculated insights, and segments are three capabilities built on top of the unified data model
Tableau Next queries Salesforce objects directly and does not depend on Data 360
CRM Analytics cannot use any Data Cloud data; the two platforms are completely separate
questions.explain: Data Cloud and Data 360 are the same product under different names. Data moves ingest (stream) → store (DLO) → harmonize (DMO) → aggregate (CIO), and identity resolution, calculated insights, and segments build on top of that unified model. Tableau Next does not connect to Salesforce objects directly — it reads Data 360 objects through a semantic model. CRM Analytics can also work with Data Cloud data, so the two platforms are not fully separate.

questions.prompt: Match each analytics tool to where its data actually comes from, per the "how the pieces fit together" lesson.
right: Data 360 objects, modeled through a semantic layer
Its own datasets, extracted and prepared inside the platform (though it can also work with Data Cloud data)
questions.explain: Native reports query live Salesforce records directly. CRM Analytics builds and queries its own prepared datasets. Tableau Next reads Data 360 objects through a semantic model. Remembering this table is the fastest way to diagnose why two tools disagree on a number: they're reading from different layers.

questions.prompt: A regional sales manager wants a weekly list of open opportunities over $50K, grouped by owner, that's always current. Per Chapter 1's decision framework, which tool should you recommend, and why?
options: Native reports and dashboards, because the data volume is small, the need is purely operational, and a more powerful platform adds cost and complexity without benefit
CRM Analytics, because any request that involves grouping should use a platform built for aggregation
Tableau Next, because it is the newest product and Salesforce is steering all new development toward it
Tableau Desktop, because it has the most mature authoring environment of the four
questions.explain: This request has small volume, lives entirely inside Salesforce, needs no blending or heavy calculation, and must stay live. That's exactly the sweet spot of native reports. Choosing a bigger platform here would mean recipes to maintain and a refresh schedule to monitor for no real benefit — the lesson's common-mistakes list calls out choosing the newest tool by default as exactly this error.

questions.prompt: Which statement about CRM Analytics datasets is correct?
options: A dataset is a copy of data — extracted, prepared, and stored inside CRM Analytics in a compressed form — not a Salesforce object, so it never appears in native reports
A dataset is a live view into Salesforce objects, queried fresh by CRM Analytics every time a dashboard loads, which is why it doesn't appear in native reports
A dataset is a Salesforce custom object that CRM Analytics creates and registers automatically in Setup, visible in Object Manager alongside your other custom objects
A dataset only exists while a dashboard using it stays open, and gets discarded the moment the dashboard closes
A dataset must contain only Salesforce data, since external or CSV sources can never be loaded into one
A dataset and a dataflow are simply two names for the exact same CRM Analytics asset
questions.explain: A dataset is prepared data, extracted and loaded into CRM Analytics and stored in a compressed, indexed form built for fast aggregation. It is not a Salesforce object, it does not show up in Object Manager, and it persists independently of any one dashboard being open. It can combine Salesforce data with external sources. A dataflow, by contrast, is one of the tools (along with recipes) that builds a dataset — the two are not the same thing.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B gets the consequence right (it doesn't appear in native reports) but swaps the actual mechanism: a dataset is a stored, prepared copy loaded on a schedule, not a live query against Salesforce objects. That one substitution — 'live view, queried fresh' instead of 'extracted and stored' — is the entire architectural point of the lesson, and it's also why dataset data can go stale while a native report never does.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in a dataflow's JSON definition, the action that extracts fields from a Salesforce object is called ________, and the action that saves the result as a dataset is called sfdcRegister.
questions.explain: sfdcDigest extracts fields from a Salesforce object into the dataflow, and sfdcRegister saves the resulting data as a dataset. sfdcDigest always comes first in the chain of named nodes; sfdcRegister is what actually produces a queryable dataset at the end.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of how data moves through CRM Analytics, per the architecture lesson, in the correct order.
items: Connect: data is brought in from Salesforce objects and external sources
Prepare: raw data is cleaned, joined, and reshaped with recipes or dataflows
Store: the result is written as a dataset, in a compressed, indexed form
Explore and visualize: lenses and dashboards query the dataset
Share: dashboards and lenses are shared through an app
questions.explain: Salesforce's own framing — connect any data, explore and visualize, share the story — expands into this five-stage chain: connect the sources, prepare them into shape, store the result as a dataset, let lenses and dashboards explore and visualize it, then share through an app. Every later topic in this course, from refresh schedules to row-level security, attaches to one specific link in this chain.

questions.prompt: A recipe joins Opportunity, Account, and User inputs, and the row count in the preview is much larger than expected after the join. Select every statement below that correctly describes how to think about this, per the Recipes lesson.
options: A join node combines two sources on matching keys, and an unexpectedly large row count often means the join key isn't actually unique on one side, producing a fan-out
The data preview shows a sample of rows (the tutorial cites up to 2,000), so checking the preview is a reasonable way to catch this before scheduling the recipe
Transform nodes, not join nodes, are what combine two sources, so a join node can't be the cause of a row-count problem
Because a recipe is drawn as a graph, you can trace which input node and which join actually produced the inflated row count
Recipes can't be previewed before they run on a schedule, so the only way to check is to let it run in production first
questions.explain: A join combines two sources on matching keys; when one side isn't actually unique on that key, each match multiplies rows, which is the classic cause of an inflated join result. The recipe's live preview (up to roughly 2,000 sample rows) exists exactly so you can catch this before scheduling it, and because the recipe is drawn as a graph, you can click back through the nodes to find where the row count jumped. Join nodes, not transform nodes, are what combine sources, and previewing is available well before anything runs on a schedule.

questions.prompt: You click one bar in a CRM Analytics dashboard chart, and a number tile and a table on the same page instantly narrow to match the selection, with no query edited by anyone. What is this behavior called, and what has to be true for it to work automatically?
options: Faceting; the widgets must share the same dataset
Binding; the widgets must be connected by a selection binding written in SAQL
Drilling; the chart must have a Drill Into This By action configured
Caching; the dashboard must already have been opened once in the session
questions.explain: This is faceting: when a viewer selects something on one widget, every other widget built on the same dataset automatically re-filters. It needs no SAQL and no manual binding — it only requires that the widgets query the same dataset. Bindings are the hand-built mechanism used when faceting's automatic behavior isn't enough, for example to connect widgets across different datasets.

questions.prompt: What does this SAQL query return?
options: For each distinct OwnerName, the total Amount of only that owner's Closed Won opportunities
The total Amount across all opportunities, labeled by whichever owner's row happens to load first
Every row in the Opps dataset where StageName equals Closed Won, with no aggregation applied
An error, because filter must come after group, not before it
questions.explain: The filter runs first and narrows the stream to only Closed Won rows. The group then buckets what's left by OwnerName, and foreach ... generate produces one row per owner with the sum of that owner's Amount. Filtering before grouping, exactly like a WHERE clause running before GROUP BY, is a legal and common pattern — there's no requirement that filter come after group.

questions.prompt: This query fails to run correctly. What is actually wrong with the statement order?
options: order references 'Cnt' before foreach ... generate has created that column — generate must come before anything that uses the columns it produces
group must come after foreach ... generate, not before it
limit must always be the very first statement in a SAQL query
load cannot be followed directly by group; a filter statement is required in between
questions.explain: SAQL is a pipeline: each statement only has access to columns that already exist in the stream it receives. 'Cnt' is defined by the foreach ... generate statement, so order can't reference it until generate has already run. The fix is to move order after foreach ... generate. group must come before foreach ... generate (not after), limit can appear anywhere once the stream is ready, and filter is never required between load and group.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how SAQL differs from SQL and SOQL, per the language-comparison lesson?
options: SAQL has a JOIN keyword identical to SQL's, while SOQL uses cogroup instead of a join
SOQL queries CRM Analytics datasets directly, while SAQL queries live Salesforce objects in real time
SAQL is a pipeline of statements, each taking an input stream and producing an output stream, so statement order is meaningful — unlike SQL and SOQL, which are declarative with a fixed clause order

SAQL is a pipeline of statements, each taking an input stream and producing an output stream, so statement order is meaningful — exactly like SQL and SOQL, which are also read and executed as an ordered sequence of pipeline steps
All three languages require data to already be loaded into a CRM Analytics dataset before any of them can run a query
In SAQL, the group statement alone defines the final output columns, with no further statement needed afterward
questions.explain: SQL and SOQL are declarative: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, and ORDER BY occur in one fixed clause order, regardless of how you arrange them conceptually. SAQL instead reads as a sequence of statements, each taking an input stream and producing an output stream, so where you place a statement — for example a filter before or after group — actually changes what it does, much like WHERE versus HAVING. SAQL uses cogroup for combining datasets, not JOIN; SAQL queries CRM Analytics datasets rather than live objects (that's SOQL's job); and group alone produces nothing usable without a following foreach ... generate.
questions.distractorExplain: Option 4 states the exact same pipeline mechanics as the correct answer — input stream, output stream, order matters — but then claims SQL and SOQL work the same way. They don't: SQL and SOQL are declarative statements with a fixed clause order, not a sequence of steps you can reorder to change behavior. That one claim, that SQL/SOQL 'also' behave as an ordered pipeline, is the entire point SAQL is contrasted against, which is what makes this the closest wrong answer.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a text widget should display the currently selected owner's name, or say "All" if nothing is selected. The expression cell(Owner_1.selection, 0, "Owner").asString() supplies the selected name, and the function that supplies the "All" default when the selection comes back empty is ________().
questions.explain: coalesce() returns the first non-empty value in the list you give it. Wrapping a binding expression in coalesce(binding_result, "All") means the widget shows the real selection when one exists, and falls back to "All" the moment the binding comes back empty — exactly the empty-selection case the bindings lesson warns you to always plan for.

questions.prompt: Match each CRM Analytics interactivity concept, from Chapter 3, to what it actually does.
right: Reads what the user picked in another step, such as a filter or a clicked chart bar
Reads the results of another step's query, such as a total or a top value
Automatically filters other widgets on the same dataset when a selection is made
Takes the viewer somewhere else, such as opening the underlying Salesforce record
questions.explain: Faceting is the automatic, no-code filtering between widgets that share a dataset. A selection binding follows what a user chose in another step; a results binding follows what another step's query returned. Actions are the odd one out — they don't change what the dashboard shows, they take the viewer somewhere else entirely, such as a Salesforce record or a global action.

questions.prompt: Three systems each hold a record for the same customer under three different emails. Which of Data Cloud's four jobs is responsible for deciding these are one person?
options: Ingest
Harmonize
Unify (identity resolution)
Analyze and act
questions.explain: Ingest brings the three records in, and harmonize maps their fields into a common model — but neither step decides whether the records describe the same person. That decision belongs to the unify stage, where identity resolution's match rules evaluate the records and link them into one unified profile.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about identity resolution rulesets, per the Identity Resolution lesson.
options: Match rules decide which profiles are the same entity; reconciliation rules decide which value wins when sources disagree
Multiple match rules within one ruleset are combined with AND, so a record must satisfy every rule in the ruleset to be unified
The unified profile is a new layer on top; source records are not deleted or overwritten
A barely-changed count between source and unified records can be a sign that the match rules are too strict
Reconciliation rules are set at the field level only, and can never be overridden at the object level
questions.explain: Match rules decide who's the same entity; reconciliation rules decide whose value survives when sources disagree. Multiple match rules within a ruleset are combined with OR, not AND — a record can match through any single rule. The unified profile sits on top of, and never deletes, the source records, which is why you can always trace a unified profile back to its sources. A source-to-unified count that barely moves is exactly the sign the lesson warns about: rules too strict to catch real duplicates. Reconciliation is set at the object level by default, with field-level overrides available — the reverse of what one option claims.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a calculated insight's SQL definition groups rows by its ________ — the attributes you group by, such as customer or region — while its aggregated values, such as a sum of order totals, are called measures.
questions.explain: Dimensions are the attributes a calculated insight groups by (customer, region, month); measures are the aggregated values computed per group (a sum, a count). Together, measures and dimensions define the insight's grain — exactly the GROUP BY columns versus aggregated SELECT columns you already know from T-SQL.

questions.prompt: A segment on the Account object has one filter container stating "a Sales Order Product record where category equals Outdoor, count at least 1" and a separate second container stating "a Sales Order Product record where quantity is greater than 10." Per the Segments lesson, what does splitting these into two containers (instead of one) mean for which accounts qualify?
options: The two conditions can be satisfied by two different related Sales Order Product records, not necessarily the same one
The two conditions must both be true of the exact same Sales Order Product record
Using two separate containers is invalid, and the segment will fail to publish
Only the first container's conditions are ever evaluated; the second is ignored
questions.explain: The segment builder's container logic matters more than it looks: conditions placed inside one container are evaluated against the same related record, while conditions in separate containers can each be satisfied by a different related record. Here, an account with one Outdoor order of quantity 2 and a separate Office-supplies order of quantity 15 would still qualify, because the two conditions live in different containers — which is rarely what the segment's author actually intended.

questions.prompt: Match each Data Cloud / Data 360 object to its role in the ingest-to-insight pipeline.
right: Cube-style metric with measures and dimensions, computed after processing
The configured connection that ingests one source object
Where ingested data lands, kept as it arrived, unaltered
A standardized structure that one or more DLOs are mapped into
questions.explain: The pipeline runs ingest → store → harmonize → aggregate. A data stream is the configured connection that ingests a source. A DLO is the raw landing zone, kept as it arrived. A DMO is the standardized structure DLOs get mapped into. A CIO is the cube-style, pre-aggregated metric computed from the harmonized model.

questions.prompt: In Tableau Desktop, two analysts might each define "Revenue" differently in their own separate workbooks. Which Tableau Next building block is specifically meant to prevent that?
options: The workspace
The semantic model
The visualization builder
The dashboard
questions.explain: A semantic model, built once in the Semantic Model Builder, holds field definitions, relationships, aggregations, and calculations centrally. Every visualization and dashboard that references it inherits the same definitions, so no author redefines "Revenue" on their own. A workspace is just the container the model lives in; the builder and the dashboard consume the model rather than governing it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about connecting Tableau Desktop or Tableau Cloud to a Tableau Next semantic model through the Tableau Semantics connector.
options: You authenticate against your Salesforce org and select a semantic model as the data source
Extracts work exactly as they do with any other Desktop data source
Several authoring features are limited when connected this way, including sets, data blending, and context filters
Changes to core semantic model fields happen at the source, not inside your workbook
The connector requires Data 360 to be fully disconnected from CRM Analytics before it will work
questions.explain: The Tableau Semantics connector has you enter your org URL, authenticate, and pick a semantic model, after which Desktop builds on the model's existing fields and definitions. Because the connection relies on the live source model rather than an extract, extracts are not available through it, and several authoring features — sets, data blending, and context filters among them — are limited. Core field changes happen at the source. Nothing about the connector requires Data 360 and CRM Analytics to be disconnected from each other; that isn't a real constraint the lesson describes.

questions.prompt: A colleague shared a Tableau Next workspace with you as a Viewer, but a dashboard inside it shows no data for you. Per the Publishing lesson, which layer should you check first, and why?
options: Data permissions in Data 360 — sharing a workspace does not share the data model objects its assets depend on, which are governed separately
Your browser cache — workspace sharing always takes a few hours to propagate
The dashboard's faceting setting — Viewer access disables faceting by default
The semantic model's YAML view — only Editors can render YAML-backed dashboards
questions.explain: The lesson's explicit trap: sharing analytics is not sharing data. Being added as a Viewer on a workspace gives you access to open the asset, but access to the underlying Data 360 objects is controlled separately through data space and object/field permissions. A Viewer who lacks those data permissions can open the dashboard and still see no data.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Tableau Next's three Agentforce analytics skills are Data Pro, Concierge, and ________ — the one that monitors metrics and proactively alerts people to changes, such as a threshold being crossed.
questions.explain: Data Pro helps build semantic models faster. Concierge answers business questions in natural language for people consuming analysis. Inspector monitors metrics and alerts people when something changes, such as a threshold crossed or an unusual trend — a capability the lesson notes was labeled beta at the time of writing.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what a semantic layer is for, per Chapter 6?
options: It is a governed layer, sitting between raw data and consuming tools, that defines business logic such as metrics and relationships once, so every dashboard and AI assistant reuses the same definitions
It is a caching layer that only exists to make dashboards load faster, with no effect on how numbers are defined
It is a feature exclusive to CRM Analytics, with no equivalent in Tableau Next
It is a one-time migration step used only when converting a dataflow to a recipe
questions.explain: A semantic layer sits between the raw/modeled data and the tools that consume it, holding business-friendly names, relationships, calculations, and official metrics defined once. Consumers — dashboards, ad hoc exploration, and AI assistants alike — ask for "Revenue by Region" and get the same governed answer instead of each re-deriving its own version. It's a Tableau Next and Data 360 construct (Tableau Semantics), not a CRM Analytics feature, and it has nothing to do with converting a dataflow to a recipe.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of writing a trustworthy metric definition, per the Defining Metrics & KPIs lesson, in the order the lesson says to work through them, before ever opening the builder.
items: Write the business question the metric answers, and who owns the answer
Decide the measure: which field is aggregated, and how
Decide the filters: which records actually count
Decide the time dimension: which date defines the period
Decide the breakdowns: which dimensions people should be able to slice by
questions.explain: The lesson's five-line discipline runs: name the business question and its owner, pick the measure and its aggregation, decide which records count through filters, settle which date defines the time period, and finally decide what breakdowns consumers get to slice by. If you can't write all five lines before opening the builder, the lesson says you aren't ready to publish the metric.

questions.prompt: A picklist stage "Negotiation" is renamed to "Contract Review." The Closed Won Revenue metric, filtered on stage = "Closed Won," still matches last month's number exactly. Per the Avoiding Metric Drift lesson, which other metric is now at risk, and from which of the four causes of drift?
options: An Open Pipeline metric that filters on the old stage name "Negotiation" — a source change, because the metric's logic is unchanged but its inputs are not
The Closed Won Revenue metric itself — silent redefinition, because someone edited it without telling consumers
No metric is at risk, because renaming a picklist value never affects any existing filter
The Win Rate metric — ambiguous time and grain, because fiscal and calendar quarters now disagree
questions.explain: This is the source-changes cause of drift: an admin changed a picklist value, the metric logic itself didn't change, but any metric whose filter still references the old stage name "Negotiation" now silently stops matching real rows. Closed Won Revenue is unaffected because "Closed Won" wasn't renamed — but an Open Pipeline metric built on "Negotiation" would quietly undercount from the moment of the rename, with no error to flag it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about metric governance roles, per Chapter 6.
options: The Owner is typically a business function, such as Revenue Operations, rather than whoever happened to build the metric
Editors should be a small, deliberately limited group, since keeping that role rare is what protects the definitions
Consumers should generally be able to use a metric but not alter its definition
Every metric, including small exploratory calculations, needs the full five-step change process before anyone can use it
questions.explain: Governance assigns a named business owner (not necessarily the builder), keeps the Editor role small to protect the definitions, and lets everyone else consume without altering. The lesson explicitly says to keep governance proportionate: govern metrics that appear in executive reporting, compensation, or external commitments, and leave exploratory analyst work alone until it becomes widely used.

questions.code:
SELECT Id, Name, Amount, SystemModstamp
FROM Opportunity
WHERE SystemModstamp > 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z
questions.prompt: This incremental-pull query, run nightly against the Salesforce REST API, reliably fetches records that changed since the last run. What does it fail to catch, and why?
options: Deleted records — a deleted row simply stops appearing in query results instead of showing up as a changed row
Records with a NULL Amount — SystemModstamp filtering silently excludes any row with a missing Amount
Records owned by inactive users — SystemModstamp only updates for records owned by active users
Nothing; this query correctly captures every kind of change, including deletions
questions.explain: SystemModstamp-based incremental filtering catches updates and new records, because both touch the field. A deletion doesn't update SystemModstamp on a surviving row — the record just stops appearing in the result set at all, so a purely timestamp-based pull never learns it happened. Deleted records need separate handling, such as syncing the IsDeleted flag or periodically comparing the full set of Ids.

questions.prompt: Per the Salesforce + dbt lesson, select every statement that correctly describes a job the staging layer needs to do for raw, replicated Salesforce tables.
options: Filter out rows where IsDeleted is true, if the ingestion tool syncs that flag, so deleted opportunities stop being counted
Deduplicate on Id, keeping the latest SystemModstamp, since some loaders can land the same Id more than once
Rename custom fields such as Region__c to a cleaner name like region
Add an accepted_values test on picklist columns such as StageName, so an admin adding a new stage is caught before a dashboard breaks
Assume every replicated formula field stays current automatically, since Salesforce formula values always replicate correctly
questions.explain: Salesforce's quirks belong in the staging layer: filter soft-deleted rows, deduplicate incremental-load duplicates on Id by latest SystemModstamp, rename the __c custom-field suffixes into clean names, and test picklist columns against the real accepted values so an admin's new stage breaks a test instead of a dashboard. Formula fields are the opposite of a safe assumption — whether they replicate, and stay current, depends entirely on the ingestion tool, so the lesson says to verify or recompute them, never assume.

questions.prompt: A team needs Data 360 to query Snowflake data where it already lives, without copying it, and specifically wants to avoid paying for Snowflake compute on those queries. Which Data 360 federation style should they choose, and what does it require?
options: File federation — Data 360 reads the data files directly, which for Snowflake requires tables managed as Apache Iceberg tables on AWS or Azure
Query federation — Snowflake's own compute answers the queries, and the Snowflake bill reflects that usage
Zero-copy data sharing — Salesforce's unified data is pushed out for Snowflake users to join with their own tables
Classic extract and load — a scheduled pipeline job copies Snowflake tables into Data 360
questions.explain: Query federation runs on Snowflake's own compute, so it's exactly the path that costs Snowflake compute. File federation instead has Data 360 read the underlying storage directly with its own compute, bypassing Snowflake's compute entirely — but the lesson notes it requires the data be stored as Apache Iceberg tables on AWS or Azure, a stricter prerequisite than query federation's. Zero-copy data sharing is the reverse direction (sharing Salesforce data out), and extract-and-load is a full copy, not a federation approach at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: for a security predicate to restrict an external, non-Salesforce dataset by user or team, the dataset needs a column that maps each row to that user or team — because, unlike Salesforce object data, external data has no Salesforce ________ or sharing rules attached to it.
questions.explain: Salesforce record sharing protects Salesforce objects because every record has an owner and inherits roles and sharing rules. Data that arrived from a warehouse or a CSV has no Salesforce owner at all, so none of that protection applies automatically — a security predicate needs an explicit mapping column before it can restrict those rows by user or team.

questions.prompt: Match each Salesforce integration mechanism to the job it fits best, per the API-Based Integration Basics lesson.
right: Authenticates a server-to-server integration that doesn't depend on a human logging in
Small, interactive requests, such as querying with SOQL or updating a few records
Large asynchronous jobs for loading or extracting big tables
Near-real-time notification of changes as they happen, instead of polling on a schedule
questions.explain: The rule of thumb from the lesson: small and interactive favors REST, big and scheduled favors Bulk, and near-real-time favors streaming/CDC. None of those three move data without credentials, which is OAuth 2.0's job — issuing short-lived, scoped tokens to a registered application so the integration authenticates without a person clicking through a login screen.

questions.prompt: A dataset built from the Opportunity object needs row-level security. Which statement correctly describes the relationship between sharing inheritance and a custom security predicate for this dataset, per Chapter 8?
options: Sharing inheritance and security predicates are two different names for the exact same CRM Analytics mechanism
A security predicate can only be used on datasets built from external, non-Salesforce data — never on a dataset built from Opportunity

Sharing inheritance can reuse the Salesforce sharing rules already built for Opportunity, and because it fully replaces the need for a predicate, no fallback predicate should ever be set on the same dataset
Row-level security in CRM Analytics is controlled entirely through app-level sharing roles; datasets have no separate row-level mechanism of their own

Sharing inheritance can reuse the Salesforce sharing rules already built for Opportunity, but Salesforce's own guidance says to also set a security predicate as a fallback, since inheritance can't always be honored
Sharing inheritance applies automatically to any dataset, no matter how many different Salesforce objects it was built from
questions.explain: Sharing inheritance lets a dataset reuse the sharing logic Salesforce already enforces for its source object, saving you from re-encoding role hierarchies as a predicate. But it has real limits — among them, a dataset can only inherit from one Salesforce object, and inheritance can't always be honored for every user's access. That's exactly why Salesforce's own documentation says to set a security predicate as a fallback alongside inheritance, not instead of it.
questions.distractorExplain: Option 3 (index 2) states the first half correctly — sharing inheritance reuses Opportunity's sharing rules — but then concludes that this fully replaces the need for a predicate and that no fallback should ever be set. That's the opposite of Salesforce's documented guidance: inheritance can't always be honored, which is precisely why a fallback predicate is recommended on the same dataset, not forbidden on it.

questions.prompt: This security predicate is applied to an Opportunity detail dataset, and no row in the dataset has a blank Region. A rep whose Region_Scope__c field is blank opens the dashboard. Which rows does the predicate return for that rep?
options: Only rows where OwnerId matches the rep's own user Id, since the second clause can't match a blank Region_Scope__c against any real Region value in the data
Every row in the dataset, because an OR condition with a blank operand automatically evaluates to true
No rows at all, because comparing against a blank Region_Scope__c causes the whole predicate to error
Only rows where Region itself is blank, since a blank value matches a blank value
questions.explain: The predicate is an OR of two clauses. For this rep, Region_Scope__c is blank, so the second clause compares the dataset's real Region values (never blank, by design) against blank — which never matches. Only the first clause, the ownership check, can be true, so the rep sees only rows they own. This is exactly the leak the capstone's security lesson warns about: if a dataset row's Region were ever accidentally blank, it would wrongly match a rep with a blank scope too, which is why that check belongs in the test matrix.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Event Monitoring for CRM Analytics, per the Auditing Analytics Access lesson.
options: Wave Interaction records what users did in the interface and how long they spent, captured when a tab is closed
Wave Change records page and route changes, such as opening a new asset
Event logs are exposed through the EventLogFile object and can be queried with SOQL
Audit logs record which specific rows of data a user saw, not just that they opened a dashboard
Event Monitoring is typically licensed separately from base Salesforce
questions.explain: Wave Interaction logs in-interface activity and time spent, captured on tab close; Wave Change logs page and route changes; both are exposed through the queryable EventLogFile object; and Event Monitoring is usually a separately licensed add-on. The lesson is explicit about the limit, though: audit logs record that a dashboard was opened, not which specific rows a predicate let that user see — proving the row-level result relies on predicate design and testing, not audit data.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: once personal data is copied out of Salesforce into a warehouse or a CRM Analytics dataset, Salesforce's sharing model and field-level security no longer protect it — so the first governance step before copying anything is to ________ the fields, recording their sensitivity and compliance category.
questions.explain: Classifying fields — tagging them by sensitivity and compliance category, using Salesforce's data classification metadata where it exists — is the starting inventory for every later governance decision: what to minimize, what to mask, and what needs tighter access once it's copied somewhere Salesforce's own controls no longer reach.

questions.prompt: In the Cobalt Ridge capstone, the quarterly new-business target is stored in its own small Targets dataset rather than hard-coded into a dashboard tile's formula. Why does that design choice matter?
options: A target hard-coded into a tile silently goes stale when the real target changes, and the coverage tile would then compare pipeline against the wrong gap without anyone noticing
CRM Analytics tiles cannot contain numeric literals at all, so a separate dataset is technically required
SAQL queries are not allowed to reference more than one dataset at a time, so the target has to live separately
Storing the target as data instead of a formula is purely a refresh-speed optimization, with no effect on correctness
questions.explain: A quarterly target typed into a formula is exactly the kind of number that quietly ages: the moment leadership resets the target, every tile that hard-coded the old figure is wrong, and nothing flags it. Storing the target as its own small dataset means updating one row updates every tile and metric that reads it, and the lesson calls this out as a deliberate improvement over the native-report habit of hard-coding a quota.

questions.prompt: This is the Cobalt Ridge bar-chart query from the capstone build lesson. Its three regions sum to $5.2M, matching the Closed Won number tile exactly. What would it mean if those two numbers did NOT agree?
options: The tile and the chart's query are built on different filters, or different versions of the dataset, and the fix belongs in the recipe or the shared query logic — not patched directly on the chart
Nothing meaningful; SAQL aggregates are expected to drift slightly from tile totals due to rounding
The dataset would need to be deleted and rebuilt entirely, since CRM Analytics has no way to recover from a mismatch
'IsWon' would need to change from a string comparison to a numeric comparison
questions.explain: The capstone's reconciliation step exists exactly to catch this: if the regional breakdown and the headline tile disagree, the two queries aren't actually computing the same thing — a missing filter, a different fiscal-quarter boundary, or a stale dataset version is the usual cause. The lesson's explicit rule is to fix it in the recipe or the shared definition, never by patching the number directly on the chart, because a chart-level patch drifts again the next time the data refreshes.

questions.prompt: Cobalt Ridge has $5.2M Closed Won against an $8.0M target, $6.0M of open pipeline closing this quarter, and a trailing win rate of 27%. Per the wrap-up lesson's forecasting logic, roughly how much pipeline coverage would actually be needed to expect to close the remaining gap, and why does the raw 2.1x coverage figure overstate how safe things look?
options: About 3.7x (1 divided by 0.27), because at a 27% win rate only roughly a quarter of open pipeline is expected to convert, and simple pipeline-to-gap coverage ignores the win rate entirely
About 2.1x is already sufficient, because coverage ratios are already calculated after applying the win rate
About 1.0x, because coverage only needs to equal the gap once a deal exists in the pipeline at all
About 0.27x, because the win rate should be multiplied directly against the coverage ratio the tile displays
questions.explain: Pipeline coverage as shown — open pipeline divided by the remaining gap — says nothing about how much of that pipeline will actually close. At a 27% win rate, expected closed dollars from $6.0M of pipeline is only about $1.6M, not $6.0M, so reaching the $2.8M gap with real confidence takes roughly 1 / 0.27 ≈ 3.7x coverage, not 2.1x. The lesson's point is that a comfortable-looking ratio can hide a real shortfall once the win rate is actually applied.

questions.prompt: Put these four stages of the Cobalt Ridge capstone build, per the kickoff lesson, in the order they're meant to happen.
items: Build the app: recipes turn Salesforce data into a dataset, and a dashboard answers the sales questions
Model the metric layer: define the headline metrics once, centrally, with owners and definitions
Connect Data Cloud: bring in product usage and surface renewal risk next to the pipeline
Secure it: apply row-level security, app sharing, and a test plan
questions.explain: The capstone builds in this order on purpose: first get a working app with real numbers, then define those numbers centrally so they can't drift, then extend the app with usage data the CRM alone can't supply, and only then lock down who sees what. Securing a dashboard before it has real content and metrics to protect would mean testing against numbers that are still about to change.
